posts.author: hamilton
posts.text: Apparently the Waterboys recorded enough material for four albums in between This Is The Sea and the final release of Fisherman's Blues.  The bonus disc on the new remaster gathers another 60-odd minutes of those sessions that didn't make the cut - and they aren't rough demos or live versions or anything like that.  And only two of the tracks are alternate versions of songs on the original album - both of which are drastically different enough from the versions on the original album to warrrant inclusion.  There's another album out there somewhere called Too Close To Heaven: The Unreleased Fisherman's Blues Sessions which apparently completes the recordings.  I guess this is their Basement Tapes.

After an initial blitz on America in the early months of 1969, when Led Zeppelin primarily opened for other acts, they return in April for their second assault. In Led Zeppelin history, no run of shows is more legendary that these four nights in San Francisco.

This is the first set of the last night of that run. After the brief comment "This is the last night" from Robert Plant, they kick off the show with the Yardbirdsâ€™ classic, "The Train Kept A-Rollin." During the following "I Can't Quit You," Plant incorporates improvised lyrics that state what a great time they were having in San Francisco. They then embark on a vicious excursion through an 18 minute "As Long as I Have You." This unreleased song was never played with more enthusiasm, and it features nods to various blues obscurities, as well as Spirit's "Fresh Garbage," while Page pummels the audience into submission.

The mood relaxes a bit with "You Shook Me" before they journey to the outer realms again for a take on "How Many More Times" that leaves the audience delirious after 22 minutes. An unusually bluesy arrangement of "Communication Breakdown" closes the first set.

Years before punk deconstructed popular music as a violent protest against the bloated rock â€˜n' roll dinosaurs staggering from stadium to stadium, Bruce Springsteen was earnestly providing his own alternative to bone-headed riffing and cowbell solos, putting out albums that echoed a simpler time while thoughtfully chronicling the plight of the workinâ€™ man on his eternal quest for Saturday Night.

Concentrating on material from their recent release, Darkness on the Edge of Town, Springsteen and his crew lay into the first half of this set with reckless abandon, reserving the early hits and holiday cheer for the second half. As soon as they take the stage, itâ€™s all lost love and drag races and full-throttle rock â€˜n' roll; then factory walls and plaintive piano with dusty, wheezing harmonica. This is the whole history of 20th century America set to music, geared up and rolling down the highway â€˜till everyone, audience included, is ready to pass out.
